utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today, Monday, the 2nd of April, I'd like to greet everyone present to the courtroom, the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and all those assisting us in our work. First of all, there are three oral decisions I would like to render. These concern the admission of documents into evidence. The first document concerns evidence presented when the witness Ferida Likic testified on the 22nd of March, 2007. The Chamber hereby decides to admit into evidence the following documents through the IC 00508 list, given that they have a certain probative value and a certain relevance. The Chamber would like to point out that documents P 06314, P 08382, P 08652, P 08660, P 08662, and P 08663 have already been admitted. They were admitted on the 29th of March, 2007. And now for the second oral decision that concerns evidence presented during the testimony of Witness DG, who appeared on the 20th of March, 2007. The Chamber hereby decides to admit the following documents presented by the Prosecution through the IC 00502 list, given that they have a certain probative value and a certain relevance. The third oral decision that concerns documents presented in the course of Mr. Mustafa Hadrovic's testimony, who appeared on the 21st and 22nd of February, 2007. Hadrovic, H-a-d-r-o-v-i-c. The Chamber hereby admits into evidence the following documents presented by the Prosecution through the IC 00445 list, and documents presented by the Defence through the IC 00446 list, given that they have a certain probative value. I would also like to remind the Prosecution that on the 8th of March, 2007, I requested that they file a list -- or, rather, a definitive witness list. I'm still waiting for this list to be submitted. It's necessary for us to have such a list in order to see which witnesses the Chamber might call if the Prosecution doesn't put these witnesses on their list. I would also like to remind the Defence that they should respond to the motion for protective measures pursuant to Rule 70, and this concerns the witness BH. I would first like two IC numbers to be provided by the registrar and then we will go into private session for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Nelson Draper. The list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 517, while the list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 518. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, let's go into private session for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just a minute. We'll move back into private session. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] No, it's not a problem; we can remain in open session. Last time you said the accused would have the right to address certain matters, the mentioned -- the meeting on the 22nd of March, and I think that I would like to express my position with regard to this matter, and on Thursday one of the accused already did so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We were thinking about having a special hearing on Thursday morning so that you can express your position. Rest reassured -- rest assured we haven't forgotten about this. On Thursday morning there'll be a hearing because at 8.30 there's a Pre-Trial Conference, but it should be over by 10.00. So we could start the hearing at 10.00 and give you the floor, and if the need arises we could then continue with the witness. So rest assured we haven't forgotten about this. We'll now have the witness called into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would first like to make sure you are receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying. If so, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have been called here as a witness by the Prosecution. Could you please tell me your first and last name and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Herbert Okun. My date of birth is 27 November 1930.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you currently have a profession or do you hold a position of any kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At present I am a professorial lecturer of international relations, international institutions, and international law at the School of Advanced International Studies, SAIS, of Johns Hopkins University in Washington, DC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, have you already testified before this Tribunal or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which case did you testify in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've testified in three cases. The first the Milosevic case, then the Krajisnik case, and the third was the Mrksic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, [Interpretation] The whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, you may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd first like to provide you with some information about the procedure we will be following here. As you have already testified here on three occasions, you are familiar with the rules. You'll first have to answer the questions that the Prosecution will put to you. You have certainly met the Prosecution already. You must have met them this weekend, and once this stage has been completed the Defence counsel who are to your left may also put questions to you in the course of their cross-examination, and the accused themselves might put questions to you since they have the right to do so if they would like to address certain technical problems. The Judges, the four Judges sitting before you may in accordance with the Rules may intervene at any time to put their own questions to you but, as has so far been the case, we prefer to wait for both parties to complete their examination before we put our questions which we put to witnesses in order to clarify some of the -- your answers or in order to fill in any gaps that we may have noticed. Any gaps we may have noticed in your answers. Try and answer the questions concisely since as the procedure we are following is an oral procedure it's what is said in the course of the hearing that is important. The Prosecution, and the Defence, too, will show documents to you and ask you to comment on them. If at any point in time you don't feel well, don't hesitate to ask for a break. As a general rule we have a break every one and a half hour, and we have 20-minute breaks to allow the witness to rest, and also for technical reasons. But if you feel it necessary to have a longer break or if you feel to have -- if you feel the need to have more frequent breaks, don't hesitate to ask us to adjourn. So this depends on your wishes. And finally, if a question is not clear to you don't hesitate to ask the party putting the question to you to rephrase it. If you would like to address the Chamber at any point in time, don't hesitate to do so. This is the information I wanted to provide you to make sure that your testimony is given in the best possible conditions, and having said that I will now give the floor to the Prosecution for their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us you are Herbert Okun born on the 27th of November, 1930; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you tell us please about your educational background, what you -- completion after high school, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. I studied at Stanford University, where I received a bachelor's degree in mediaeval history in 1951. I then studied at Syracuse University in history, then at Princeton University in history, and that ended in 1952. I studied and received a master's of public administration from Harvard University in 1959, and I studied at the naval -- the US [Realtime transcript read in error "UN"] Naval War College and received a degree, a masters in naval warfare, in 1969.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Is it correct that from approximately 1955 until 1991 you served more or less continuously as an officer in the United States foreign service?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, continuously. There was no break in my service.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly, sir -- I just want to touch on some of the postings and involvements that you had prior to taking up your responsibilities in connection with Yugoslavia in the early 1990s. Can you tell the Judges briefly, did you have any role to play in your foreign service career in connection with the Cuban Missile Crisis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I -- I'm very sorry but there seems to be a mistake in the transcript. I suppose it is not a UN naval War College that you attended but a US naval ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I said US.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ambassador, could you tell us briefly about your involvement in the Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I was then second secretary at the American embassy in Moscow where I served from 1961 to '63. In October 1962, I was asked by the Ambassador to be at the ready to translate all the communications between Chairman Kruschev and President Kennedy that concerned the Cuban crisis. I had learned Russian at Stanford University and it was a language I spoke well and read comfortably. So I was asked to translate the letters between Kennedy and Kruschev, which I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And following that, can you tell us -- did you serve for a time as the deputy chair of the United States delegation at the Strategic Arms Limitation Talks with the Soviet Union, often more commonly known as SALT II?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did, from 1978 and '79.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was your -- very briefly your role in those proceedings?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, I was the deputy chairman of the American delegation, and my role principally was to draft the treaty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And is it correct, sir, that in 1973, 1974, you were a political advisor or were political advisor to the NATO commander-in-chief in the Mediterranean based in Naples with the specific responsibility -- well, first of all, did you have that position?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in the course of performing your duties in that position, did you have some responsibilities in connection with what was then Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. My principal purpose for being there was to be the Yugoslav specialist on the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges whether that was the first time officially that you had duties, foreign service duties, specifically in connection with Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Not really, because I dealt marginally but officially with Yugoslavia in my capacity, which was constant in my service dealing with the Soviet Union and with Germany. Yugoslavia was always in the arc of attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us please about your posting to the German Democratic Republic between 1980 and 1983?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I was American Ambassador to the German Democratic Republic in those years, '80 to '83, residing in what was then East Berlin, and I had the normal duties that any ambassador has.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And could you tell us what post you held during the time 1985 to 1989?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: From 1985 to 1989 I was the deputy permanent representative and ambassador of the United States to the United Nations in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us, please, what positions or functions you fulfilled or carried out during the period 1991 to 1997?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: From 1991 to 1997 I was involved principally, almost exclusively, with matters concerning the former Yugoslavia. From 1991 to 1993, I was the deputy personal envoy of the United Nations Secretary-General for the former Yugoslavia, first concerned principally with the conflict in Croatia and then principally concerned with the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina. From May 1993 to 1996, in the same capacity, I was principally occupied with mediating and resolving the Greek-Macedonian dispute over the name of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us as we've moved more closely to the time that we will talk about in the course of your testimony, what position you held during the period September 1992 until approximately May 1993?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: From September 1992 until May 1993, in addition to the regular and other tasks, I was the deputy co-chairman of the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia. This was the conference that was established at the London conference of August 1992 to bring together the efforts of the then EC and the United Nations, and the conference -- the two efforts were joined. The co-chairmen of the conference were, for the UN, the former American Secretary of State, Cyrus Vance, and for the EC, the former British Foreign Secretary, David Lord Owen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then following that term as you told us a moment ago, then you moved to your responsibilities in connection with mediating a dispute between Greece and the -- what was then the Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The official title at the United Nations was the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, usually known by the initials FYROM.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And before we move on, just for purposes of the record, and it may come up at some time or another, when you've told us that between 1991 and 1997 you were a special advisor and deputy to the personal envoy -- as a personal envoy of the United - UN, excuse me - the UN Secretary-General, who was the UN Secretary-General during that time period?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: At the beginning in 1991 the Secretary-General was Javier Perez de Cuellar, a very distinguished Peruvian diplomat. His term ended in 1991, and from January 1st, 1992, the Secretary-General was Boutros Boutros-Ghali, an equally distinguished Egyptian diplomat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And before turning further to your specific involvement in connection with Yugoslavia in 19 -- in the 1991 and 1993 time period, can you tell us again, just by way of your background, briefly your teaching positions other than the one you just mentioned a moment ago at Johns Hopkins?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, before teaching at Johns Hopkins I taught for a number of years at the Yale Law School.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On what topic or subject?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I lectured on international law and international negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, moving back specifically or forward specifically to your roles in connection with the former Yugoslavia, can you tell the Judges how you first became involved with Secretary Vance in connection with the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: In early October 1991, Secretary Vance and I were contacted separately and together by the Secretary-General and asked if we could proceed immediately to Yugoslavia in the capacity which I've mentioned. First on a fact-finding mission, and then to recommend courses of action that the United Nations and the Security Council and the Secretary-General might follow with regards to the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, which at that time was limited to the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And following that period which focused more specifically on the Republic of Croatia, did you subsequently become involved in work that focused more specifically on Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. Secretary Vance succeeded in ending the hostilities in Croatia with an accord signed on January 2, 1992, between the government of Croatia and the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army. The cessation of hostilities was effective, and, based on that accord, the United Nations surround voted in February of 1992 to establish a peacekeeping operation in Croatia. This was, I might add, the first peacekeeping operation in Europe in the history of the United Nations. But even during the Croatian period, from October 1991, Mr. Vance and I were heavily involved in the Bosnian situation because it was widely known, it was common knowledge that the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina was an explosive one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us then more specifically how you and Secretary Vance turned your attention or were given these additional specific duties in connection with Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: As I said, we maintained a watching brief on Bosnia, including visits to Sarajevo and frequent discussions with Bosnian leaders. I should mention that at that time, that is the first half of 1992, the diplomatic negotiating effort, the overall negotiating effort was totally in the hands of the EC. In the summer of 1991, the EC established, for example, a conference, a multi-lateral peace conference called the Conference on Yugoslavia headed by Lord Carrington, the former British secretary for foreign affairs, in order to achieve a peace, comprehensive peace for all of Yugoslavia if possible. The conference did not succeed, but the EC effort continued, along with Mr. Vance and me and our team of two or three other people, which was the only UN effort at the time. But in August 1992, the British government, who then held the Presidency of the EC, convened a large conference of foreign ministers in London, and at that conference it was decided to establish the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia, that is to say, as I mentioned, joining the EC effort with Secretary Vance and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On behalf of the UN.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, acting on behalf of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, before we continue on now more specifically with your work on various peace plans or in particular what became known as the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, let me ask you about certain diaries that you kept during this time which may come up in the course of your testimony or which you may refer to or others may ask you about in the course of your testimony. Were you keeping diaries during this time, 1991, 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. From the first day of our involvement in the former Yugoslavia I maintained, for myself and for Secretary Vance, a record of what was said to us, whom we met, when we met them, and it was of course useful. I should say I am not a stenographer and do not -- could not and did not take verbatim notes, but the diaries were quite complete. As a professional diplomat, one is very used to this sort of work. Accuracy is important, so I maintained these diaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just pick up on what you just said. In connection with your work in the former Yugoslavia, was that the first time in your foreign service career that you had kept diaries or had that been an established practice with you for some time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Oh, it's an established practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were these diaries -- how did you actually make the entries in your diaries? Were these collected and you put these thoughts down some days later or were they contemporaneous or how do you prepare these papers?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: They were all contemporaneous. At the negotiating table I had my notebook in front of me. I could be seen writing and taking notes. When I myself was alone with an interlocutor, I sometimes had my diary with me. Very often I didn't because it would not be polite to be writing when you're talking directly to somebody. And when that was the case, I would write it immediately after the meeting, as soon as the meeting ended. So they were done on the spot so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. You just mentioned and let me come back to it briefly before going forward, you said that you could be seen taking notes. The persons that were involved in these meetings, I take it you're indicate -- it was not a secret that you were making notes?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you use these notes in part to prepare reports on behalf of Secretary Vance and yourself to the Secretary-General of the United Nations during this time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. They formed the basis for Secretary Vance's reports, along, of course, with his own impressions and opinions and views, but they were the only record we kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me turn our attention to some of the events taking place in Yugoslavia around this time itself. Can you remind the Judges, please, when did the actual fighting between the Serbs and other non-Serb forces or persons in Bosnia-Herzegovina begin?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Except for very small-scale, random, and occasional acts of violence, the fighting began in March 1992, immediately after the referendum in Bosnia ended. It expanded significantly in April 1992 with the shelling by the Bosnian Serb army of Sarajevo, and continued until 1995 with occasional cessation -- cease-fires on various -- in various parts of the front. The heaviest fighting, I should add, was in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that this fighting took place or erupted on a large scale at least immediately after the referendum in Bosnia. Just so the record is clear, was that the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was held on the -- February of the -- excuse me, the 29th of February and March 1, 1992?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did the Serbs participate in that referendum to your knowledge, the Serb citizens of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: No. The Bosnian Serbs boycotted the referendum, and it was voted then on only by the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats. The Serbs chose not to participate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct then to understand based on what you've just told us in the last few minutes that the major outbreak of fighting then, the large-scale war gave was partly in reaction to or following the referendum results?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. The Bosnian Serbs had let it be known that they would resist the results of any referendum. Indeed, the Bosnian Serbs had already declared the existence, the self-declared existence of their self-declared state, the Republika Srpska, on January 15th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In that regard, let me ask you, in your role as an international representative during this time, what was the knowledge of the international community and persons like yourself in connection with one meeting between Tudjman and Milosevic in Karadjordjevo in March 1991 and then a meeting between Radovan Karadzic and Mate Boban in Graz in May -- sorry, if I misspoke. March 1991 was Karadjordjevo and Graz in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I would not say these meetings were widely reported or known to the general public, but those who had reason to follow events in Yugoslavia knew of these meetings and knew quite well of the meetings and knew what the subject matter of these meetings was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was the subject matter of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The subject matter was the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the principal subject -- sub-subject, ancillary subject, was the partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina between Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In carrying out your diplomatic missions during this time, Ambassador, can you tell us what you understood, what information you gained around that time of what this partition between -- of Bosnia by the Serbs and the Croats, what that might look like, what you had heard about any discussions at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. It was known at the time that the basic form of any partition, if there was to be one by Serbs and Croats, would generally follow the outline of the Cvetkovic-Macek agreement, the Sporazum, as it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was the approximate date of the Cvetkovic-Macek agreement?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The date of the agreement, the Sporazum, is August 1939.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And could you tell us a bit more about what the -- how that agreement came about, briefly, and what was the result in terms of maps or territory resulting from that agreement?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. When Yugoslavia came into being at the end of the First World War, it was not called Yugoslavia. The name of the country was the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, and the Serbian royal family became the King of the country. You see by that immediately the national emphasis of the people of the former Yugoslavia. Relations were not good in the 1920's between the principal nationalities, the Croats and the Serbs. Indeed the leading Serb [sic] politician of the time was murdered by a Serb in the parliament in the late 1920's. So in late 1929, King Aleksandar changed the name from of the country from the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes to Yugoslavia in order to de-emphasise the national aspect, and at the same time he abolished the traditional provincial borders of the country. And instead of the borders he created what were called "banovina," "banovine" or "banovinas" in English, we would say. There were nine of these Banovinas, all named after rivers of the former Yugoslavia, and again that was done in order to de-emphasise the national aspect, so that when we talk about the banovinas, the Croatian Banovina in the Cvetkovic-Macek Agreement, that is what people are talking about, and indeed there was a map. Cvetkovic and Macek created a map of what the -- what their border, what their common border would look like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Before we continue on, sir, I may have misheard or you may have misspoke or, in fact, it may be absolutely correct. You said -- a few moments ago, you said, "Indeed the leading Serb politician at the time was murdered by a Serb in the parliament"?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: No, the leading Croat politician. I excuse me, I'm sorry. The leading Croat -- Croatian politician was murdered by a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would ask the record to be corrected on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It has been, Ambassador, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, this topic could be discussed I suppose at any number of places during the course of your testimony, I suppose now is as good a time as any. In connection with the Cvetkovic-Macek agreement of 1939, was that agreement put into effect and remind us what happened soon after that.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: As I said it was signed in August 1939. Less than a month later Germany invaded Poland and World War II began. So its implementation was naturally slowed and never completed. As we will all know, Nazi Germany invaded and conquered Yugoslavia in 1941. So the Cvetkovic-Macek Agreement fell completely into disuse after April 1941 because Yugoslavia was an occupied country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what were the borders or political composition of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia during World War II?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: During the Second World War, the Nazi German government created a so-called Independent State of Croatia with its capital in Zagreb. The state was headed by the Poglavnik, that is to say the fuehrer, the leader, of the Ustasha extreme political party, and it existed under German protection. The Germans gave all of Bosnia-Herzegovina to this state so that from 1941 to 1945 the puppet State of Croatia occupied and was responsible for the activities in what is today Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did the borders of the Independent State of Croatia include or encompass all of what became -- later became Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going back with that additional background to the Graz meeting in May 1992, how did you learn or what did you know of the time about how that concept, the Banovina, related to the discussions between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Boban at that time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, press reports, and we relied in the main on press reports, spoke of the Banovina. We all knew about it. Anybody connected in any degree with the former Yugoslavia knows about the Sporazum, the agreement, because it's a datum, a fact, so that the assumption was that if the Serbs and the Croatians were talking about partitioning Bosnia, it would likely be along the lines of the agreement of 1939.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask the witness to now please be provided with the bundle of exhibits, and as that's happening and I'll ask the witness or for the Judges' information, I will ask you to look at Exhibit P 00187. And if I could ask -- if I could direct the courtroom's attention to page 4 of that set of papers. Page 4. And if that page 4 could perhaps also be put on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you in particular to look -- direct your attention to items 1 and 2. You can certainly scan the entire document, but if I can ask you to please look at 1 and 2. Is what's written here consistent with what you and Secretary Vance and others understood at the time of the discussions between Mr. Boban and Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, it is consistent. May I add, sir, that as, I read item 2, I note that the Hrvatska banovina, the Croatian Banovina, is specifically referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is that the same concept or was that the -- again the banovina that you're referring to a few moments ago as resulting from the Cvetkovic-Macek agreement from 1939?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, because the only time banovinas existed was in that period, because after Yugoslavia was liberated in 1945 the Communist Tito government created new republics and new borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in reference to the Graz Agreement of May 1992, what was your understanding, and the understanding of the international community, so far as you knew, of where this agreement left the Muslim people in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, it -- it left them really nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges in scanning through this agreement is there anyplace on the face of this document where any discussion is made about a Muslim territory or what part that Muslims would be left with?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: No. There's no mention of the Muslim community.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the people in your profession, the diplomatic corps and the international community to learning of this Graz meeting?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, as you mentioned, the meeting occurred in May 1992. By that time, there was very heavy fighting in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Bosnian Serb army already occupied more than two-thirds of the country, and the agreement was noted, but I would not say that a great deal of attention was paid to it. Those who knew the situation were not surprised to see it, but the primary activity at the time, and again I stress this, the activity of the European Community which was leading the international negotiations at the time in May 1992, the primary activity was to try and stop the Serb aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges whether -- was there further -- was there a further carrying out of this plan or a further public statements taken by either the Serb side or the Croat side as to what this meant for Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Oh, I would say constantly. It was an undercurrent of Croat and Croatian activity, and we were always aware of that. Numerous examples could be cited. Probably the most dramatic public example occurred as late as 1995 when President Tudjman was in London, and he was at a dinner, seated next to Paddy Ashdown, Lord Ashdown --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. This covers a piece of evidence that the Court has ruled to be irrelevant. It was the subject and motion by the Prosecution to admit, and in response to a Defence position the Court ruled it out on the grounds that it was irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would say this was tendered as part of the transcript of Mr. Paddy Ashdown, which was in fact received, I must say, in contrast to the Chamber's ruling, was in fact received in the Blaskic case, the Kordic case, and the Tuta-Stela case all as relevant evidence on the very same point, and this is simply a part of this witness's account of what he knew at the time and the sort of things that were openly known by the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The gentleman wasn't present, and according to Mr. Ashdown there was a lot of drinking going on. Mr. Ashdown is a known alcoholic, or at least that's what is perceived in the press. If we're going to be relying on press. And so we can bring Mr. Ashdown in here and he can be cross-examined and he can tell us what he said, but we also have to put it into context and I think if this gentleman, if he wasn't there, he cannot give us that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, leaving that aside, the -- the issue that we brought to the Court's attention was that all that had happened in this conversation was that the there was speculation as to what the status of Bosnia and Herzegovina might be in ten years' time. The dinner took place in 1995, and therefore the evidence was really dealing with a speculation on a social occasion as to what might be the condition of Bosnia in 2005, and for that reason the Court held it to be irrelevant. And whatever another Trial Chamber may have thought, that's the ruling in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber will confer and deliberate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as this dinner is concerned and everything that might relate to the dinner, it's our opinion that this should be taken as an anecdote. So it would be best for the Prosecution to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just simply note in moving on that it would have been better, in our respectful submission, rather than have counsel speculate about the nature of this testimony, for the Chamber to have heard Mr. Ashdown's testimony, which he gives a very detailed account of the map drawn by President Tudjman, partitioning Bosnia, but be that as it may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you this: In the statement that you gave a few weeks ago, you said that following Graz -- in connection with Graz and Karadjordjevo, both sides made solemn protestations for the benefit of the broader public about the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you tell us what you mean by that and how that enters into what the international community was doing at that time in reacting to this situation?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. Both the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Croats, primarily the Bosnian Croats in this case, would issue statements concerning the integrity, the sovereignty, the territorial integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they would solemnly affirm their adherence to these concepts. The Bosnian Serbs did that occasionally but a little less so, but that was not true. Their actions belied these public statements, and the international negotiators were always aware of this two-track policy. That is to say the one track in public, declaring loyalty and fielty to the independent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and on the other track working to undermine that state and establish their own political entities on the territory of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just stay on that one moment longer, sir, since you are very senior diplomat with years of experience in this area. How -- is that unique in your experience as a diplomat, sir, or how could it be that a party on the one hand?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could take a public position and at the same time to your knowledge be taken a different have a different agenda?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. It calls for speculation, and what others are doing in other parts of the world is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm asking for his -- based on his experience as a diplomat, as a senior diplomat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's still irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, according to the transcript, the question was about knowledge, not about speculation, because line 9 mentions his experience as a diplomat. So he is not being asked to speculate. The witness is being asked to say what he thinks about the matter in the light of his diplomatic knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It would still be irrelevant even if it's not speculation. How did -- how the Russians acted during the SALT agreement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The objection has been overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm still entitled to make my record.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, that was -- I was making my record, Your Honour. It's still irrelevant. How the Russians, for instance, might have negotiated during the SALT agreement or how the Greeks might have negotiated with FYROM or Macedonia or whatever you want to call or other parts of the world is irrelevant, and I just think that -- I don't see how this is relevant to this testimony. Now, perhaps you may wish to ask the Prosecutor how it -- how he thinks this is relevant information for you to consider.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas has made his record, Your Honour. Excuse me. Mr. Karnavas has made his record. The Court has ruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ambassador, could you go forward and give us your answer in terms of your professional observations and based on your more than 50 years -- 50 years of diplomatic experience on this kind of situation.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It is not uncommon to follow this kind of two-track policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Does that go for the United States as well? I mean, that's -- that's -- because this is a relevant follow-up question. Was the US also pursuing a two-track policy during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If Mr. Karnavas wants to ask that during cross-examination, he may do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's exactly what I was going to say. This is a question for cross-examination. Mr. Scott, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. We'll move on, Ambassador, and perhaps you may find as we continue on other opportunities to address that situation further. Now, you told us earlier this afternoon that in August of 1992 there was a conference in London which then, if I understand correctly, resulted in the formation of the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia, sometime referred to as the ICFY or ICFY for short; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when did ICFY then begin its work?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It began its work in Geneva immediately after the conclusion of the London conference. That means it began its work at the beginning of September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were you and Secretary Vance and Lord Owen located in Geneva during that time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, how the conference was organised and how it conducted its business?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The conference took up its work from where the EC had left off, so the acquis was part of our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you explain to those in the courtroom who may not be familiar with the word or conference, what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It's French and it's the pass participle -- in English we would say that which has been acquired. That is to say all of the previous official material is utilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: There was the -- the chair and co-chairmen's, Secretary Vance, Lord Owen and myself, and Ambassador Peter Hall, a British ambassador. We had five working groups working on various aspects of the problem. One on Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. The purpose was directly to seek to negotiate a peace accord among the parties. We had a working group on humanitarian affairs, a working group on minorities specially, a working group on economic affairs, and, hmm, there was a fifth working group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A working group on military affairs?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me. Of course. A working group on military affairs. Those were the five working groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us how the meetings, how the actual meetings with various of the parties to the conflict were conducted during this time period?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. We met continuously, nonstop, with the parties individually or bilaterally, both in Geneva and in the former Yugoslavia. You can understand naturally that much travel to Yugoslavia, the former Yugoslavia, was involved in this kind of negotiating effort while the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina raged. Between September and December, most -- the bulk of the meetings of the chairman and the co-chairman were with the individual parties. There were bilateral meetings on the whole. The reason for that was that the Bosnian Muslims would not sit down, as they said, at the same table with the Bosnian Serbs. So that naturally led to a certain course of action. After January, the broader groups met with the co-chairman and the conference took on a more even intense form after January 1992 -- excuse me, January 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Might I put a very, very small follow-up question? You have said, Ambassador, that you often met in former Yugoslavia. Could you tell it us the venues? Where was that within the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this period it was primarily Zagreb, Sarajevo, and Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm next going to ask you if you can name the principal participants or representatives of the three principal parties. I'm start with the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Who represented -- who participated in these proceedings, conferences, meetings, on behalf of the Bosnian government?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: On behalf of the Bosnian government the principal participants were President Izetbegovic, Foreign Minister Silajdzic, Ejub Ganic, General Halilovic, and Mr. Trnka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what position did Mr. Ganic hold during that time, if any?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: His positions varied. He called himself sometimes vice-president. He -- he had different denominations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was Mr. -- General Halilovic, was he there sort of the senior military representative for the Bosnian Muslim -- the government side?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us, please, then, who appeared or who were the principal representatives on behalf of the Bosnian Serbs in these meetings?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The principal representatives for the Bosnian Serbs were Radovan Karadzic, who was the self-proclaimed president of the self-proclaimed Republika Srpska; Momcilo Krajisnik, who was vice-president; Nikola Koljevic, and General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't mean to interrupt, but the previous question to that was with respect to Halilovic, whether he was with the -- starts with "military representative of the Bosnian Muslim," and then there is the government side. Now, it's either a compound question or Mr. Scott meant to correct himself, but I would like to know to this gentleman's mind: Was he there on behalf of the Muslims or was he there on behalf of the government, meaning a government that would represent everybody in Bosnia-Herzegovina, not just one side?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I would ask for a clarify questioning, but once again I would ask that counsel, and for the Court's guidance, save these matters for cross-examination, which they will have every opportunity to conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, but which party to these proceedings -- which party to these proceedings did General Halilovic represent or participate with?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He was in the dual capacity as a member of the government delegation and the Muslim leader, army leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you say "the Muslim army leader," you're referring primarily, do I take it, to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And can you please then tell the Judges who were the principal representatives or participants for the Bosnian Croat party?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: For the Bosnian Croats there was President Tudjman himself of the Republic of Croatia in Zagreb; Mate Boban, the leader of the Bosnian Croats. Mate Boban. Who else? Numerous other gentlemen. Could I consult my statement for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps I can assist you. Did Mile Akmadzic play any role in that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Ah, yes. Dr. Akmadzic played an important role that needs explaining, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Dr. Akmadzic was formally and officially the Prime Minister of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, he acted and indeed said directly to us that he was there as a representative of the Bosnian Croat side, and this was evidenced not just confidentially to the negotiators but to the world at large, because at the meetings of the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia, most of which were held in open conference rooms at the Palais des Nations in Geneva, Dr. Akmadzic sat physically with Mate Boban and the Bosnian Croat side. So there was no doubt who he represented. It was open. It was direct. It was honest. But there was an anomaly since formally he was Prime Minister of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you've mentioned in connection with the -- a military participant on behalf of each party Mr. Halilovic, Mr. Ratko Mladic, and can you tell us who was the military representative, if you will, on behalf of the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It slipped my mind. Could you refresh my memory?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We'll come back to it, if we need to, in a few minutes perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He can refresh the memory of the ambassador. There's no reason not to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If there's anything that you would like to refer to, if it would assist you, Ambassador, or perhaps in the interest of time I don't think there would be any serious dispute. I think it's a matter of public record, essentially. Was the military representative Mr. Milivoj Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a moment ago that the head of the Bosnian Croat delegation was President Franjo Tudjman, the president of the Republic of Croatia. Can you explain to the Judges, if you can, how it was that the president of the Republic of Croatia headed the delegation of Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, I should state at the outset that most of our dealings were with Mate Boban, but President Tudjman took a very active interest in the affairs of the conference and the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and made it plain to Mr. Vance and me that he, A, was in charge; B, wished to be kept informed, and; C, would be happy to deal with us on these issues. And also in conversation, everyday conversation, Mate Boban might say to me, "Yes, Mr. Ambassador, I think that's possible, but I'd have to check with President Tudjman."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to change topics. I'm looking at the clock and I'm wondering if now might be the time to take the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before we have the break, I'd like to go back to the Prosecution's question. When Mr. Mate Boban said that he had referred to President Tudjman, is that because Mr. Tudjman was the head of the delegation, as one says in diplomatic language, or because he was an observer on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not formally the head of delegation, but he was de facto the head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now have our 20-minute break. It's almost 20 to 4.00, and we will resume at 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will continue, but first I'm going to give the floor to the registrar for an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, President. 4D has submitted a list documents they wish to be tendered through witness Nelson Draper. This list for the list shall be given Exhibit number IC 519. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like, before we continue on with the work of the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia, to ask you about when did the international community or you and your particular group Lord Owen, Secretary Vance, yourself, when do you recall first becoming aware of, apart from the conflict going on with the Serbs, that there was a conflict either brewing or happening between the Croats and Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: That a conflict was brewing was known early on. I would say from the outset of the war in March 1992, and even somewhat earlier because of the spill-over from the Serb aggression against Croatia, which had understandably manifestations in Bosnia. Probably the events of Prozor in 1992 with the -- was close to the first major indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At around the time that you heard about the events in Prozor, did you hear anything about related events perhaps in the area of Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. The Novi Travnik area was very sensitive because of the large armaments factory located there, and this was brought to our attention and to the attention of many others as well. There was no secret about the fighting there, and the parties would talk about it directly to us. That is to say the government side would complain. Mate Boban for the Croats would complain. So we were aware of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In that very regard, sir, if I could ask you to look at in your are bundle of documents Exhibit P 00660. Can you look at that briefly, sir, and can you tell us do you recall having seen that document back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this is a letter from Mr. -- from President Izetbegovic to Cyrus Vance and Lord David Owen. Did this come about -- this is dated the 27th of October, 1992. Does that remind you of the approximate time period of events related to Prozor and Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. To the best of my recollection it's contemporaneous with those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Continuing on that same topic, could I ask you next to please look -- go to Exhibit P 01462. This is a report, the -- yeah, they should be all tabbed by numbers there. 1462. Apparently it's in the second binder I've just been told. My apology to the usher. There it is. Sir, if you look at that for a moment, and just -- it's a rather long document but there are some specific parts I'll direct your attention to in a moment.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you remind the Judges who -- this is a report by the Special Rapporteur, Mr. Mazowiecki. Who was Mr. Mazowiecki at this time, and what was his role in connection with -- or how did he come to be involved as the Special Rapporteur to the UN on the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Tadeusz Mazowiecki was the distinguished former Prime Minister of Poland. When he left that office, he continued his international activities, and when the United Nations decided to establish the role of a Special Rapporteur for human rights in the former Yugoslavia and specifically Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Secretary-General asked Prime Minister Mazowiecki if he would be the rapporteur, and he accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. In looking at this document, let me go, if you will, to the end and then work backwards to some extent. Can you please turn -- it would be -- the pages are numbered in the upper-left corner, and if I can please ask you to go all the way to page 76, which is Annex number III.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This makes reference to the London international conference, programme of humanitarian issues agreed between the co-chairmen to the conference and the parties to the conflict. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges whether that is reference to the conference involving Secretary Vance and Lord Owen?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. This is the London conference of August 1992 that I referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just as a couple of particular examples, if I could please direct your attention to item number 2(d), as in "dog." Can you tell the Judges one of the issues that emerged at this time was the problem of the detention of civilians?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you -- excuse me. In connection with that document, was there a signature on this programme, in fact if you go to page 78 can you tell us whether that document bears the signatures of Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Karadzic, and Mr. Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I see their names, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It says, "Identical copies of this document were signed in London on 27 August 1992 ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That was the conference in London that was held immediately preceding the formation of the then ongoing group in Geneva; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just a number of references to be followed by a couple of questions. Can I ask you to go to page 7, paragraph 16. Page 7, paragraph 16. Can you tell the Judges in reference to that entry what knowledge were you -- what knowledge and information were you, Secretary Vance, Lord Owen, and others receiving around this time in connection with so-called ethnic cleansing in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, it was a constant subject, a constant object of attention. It was being carried out very heavily by the Bosnian Serbs, particularly along the Drina and in Western Bosnia, Prijedor and that region. And the Bosnian Croats were active in ethnic cleansing around Mostar and other areas in South Herzegovina and in Central Bosnia, which is where Novi Travnik is, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I please ask you to direct your attention to page number 9, paragraph 30. I won't take everyone's time to read the entire paragraph, but the first sentence is: "There are accounts of ethnic cleansing being carried out by Croat forces in the area of Prozor toward the end of 1992." It goes on to make reference a couple of lines down to October 1992. Can you look at that paragraph, please, and my question to you: Is that information here consistent with what you told us about a few moments ago, the information that you were hearing and receiving around this time as to the outbreak of a more large-scale conflict between the Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. This is consistent with what we understood, what we knew at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I please direct your attention to paragraph 53 on page 13. You mentioned a few moments ago that one of the issues that had -- was already becoming known around this time was the detention of various ethnic persons and civilians, and this makes reference to the holding of prisoners or detainees by various groups, including approximately 894 known detainees held by Croat forces. Let me ask you to look at -- before I put a question to you, if you go on that same topic page 16, paragraph 71. "Croat forces are detaining 537 persons in four known places of detention even though their leaders had stated that they held no further detainees. They are: Livno, Mostar, Rodoc, Orasje, and Rascani." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. I might add here --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: -- that there was no attempt to hide this detention activity. The three warring parties, the -- the three warring parties met with the ICRC, the International Committee of the Red Cross, and declared their detention centres in order for the ICRC representatives to visit the camps or to try to visit the camps. They couldn't always visit. They weren't always allowed to do so. But as I say, the parties did openly declare that they held these people most -- almost all of whom were civilians, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going to another topic besides the detention of civilians, can I ask you please to look at page 23, the end of paragraph 105. "For example, Serb houses were reportedly burnt in the village of Gradina by government/Croat forces in July 1992 as were Muslim houses in Prozor by Croat forces in October 1992." Again, sir, can you tell the Judges, is that information consistent with information you and Secretary Vance and Lord Owen were receiving around that time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, the reports of the ECMM, that is to say the European Community Monitoring Mission, and by UNPROFOR, the United Nations Protective Force, were consistent with this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, moving forward, sir, and back to the particular work of the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia, in the course of carrying out your mission, did you make any efforts -- I suppose it's an obvious question, but can you tell us what you and Secretary Vance and Lord Owen and your delegation did to learn about the positions or aims, if you will, about the various principal parties to these negotiations? What were their objectives as they became known to you in the course of these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: In the first instance we discussed it directly with them very thoroughly. This was necessary because the principal task of the conference was to develop a settlement, a peaceful settlement of the conflict, and it goes without saying that one of the first things you would do in that situation is learn the objectives, seek to learn the objectives of the contending parties. So this was a steady subject of discussion. And then there were public documents. The Bosnian Serb so-called parliament would issue statements. They did issue a very important one in May 1992. The same thing went for Mate Boban and the Herceg-Bosna people, and of course the government did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, just for the record, when you're carrying out diplomatic work such as this, are you relying then only on what the parties themselves tell you and about their public positions, or what other information do you gather and draw conclusions from?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Oh, one gets them from a whole host of sources. Journalists may -- who have interviews with one of the other leaders of the parties, or one of the people in the field may tell you things that they learn. The non-governmental organisations, the NGOs, deal directly with the organisations. Madam Ogata and the United Nations -- the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, which was the lead agency for the entire UN effort in Bosnia-Herzegovina had her own sources, and she, by the way, was the chair of the working group on humanitarian affairs. So we were in steady contact with Mrs. Ogata and with her people. So there were many sources of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. With that background in mind, can you briefly describe for the Judges then, and we will go through all three of the major parties but we'll start with the Bosnian government, can you tell us what the position of President Izetbegovic and the Bosnian government were as these objectives or aims became known to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before he answers that question, Your Honour, I notice that they keep referring to this "government." Now, is it the government representing all of the people by the people, or is it the Muslims? Because I think we need some clarification. He says three parties. I think it's misleading to refer to the Muslims as "the government."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, again perhaps Mr. Karnavas would like to talk inquire about that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- to him on cross-examination, but let me just ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, during this time was an internationally recognised government of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was based in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, there was. Its independence had been recognised. It was a member of the United Nations. So there was an internally -- internationally recognised government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what were the positions or aims, if you will, as you learned then of this government?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The principal aim of the Muslim-dominated government was to create, to develop, to have a highly centralised unitary state within secure, recognised boundaries of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They hoped, or at least some members of this government wanted it to be non-ethnically based, so to speak a government of all its citizens. Others inside the government saw it more from the Muslim angle, and that was also known. And it was to be, as I say, highly centralised, and so the constituent units of the country - after all, all countries with constituent units whether they're called states or provinces or regions, whatever - they wanted these constituent units to be largely administrative and the government to be centralised with the decision-making power in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: One of the words you used a moment ago in describing this position was a unitary state or a unitary government. You said "unitary state" on line 24 at page 44.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "unitary" in this context?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: By "unitary" I mean that there was to be one state called Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with no sub-units on the territory. And the reason they were insistent on that was that the Bosnian Serbs, as I mentioned earlier, had already declared the existence in their minds of a state called Republika Srpska, and the Bosnian Croats had already declared and let it be known about the community of Herceg-Bosna, so that the government wanted a unitary statement without the existence of these sub-states.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you then tell the Judges, please, what the aims or objectives as you came to know them, you and Secretary Vance and Lord Owen - when I say "you," I'm speaking of the group of you working together, not just yourself personally - that you came to know about the positions and aims of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. The Bosnian Serbs had many aims. The first was the creation of the Republika Srpska, the Serbian republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The second was that this state should have a continuous territory, not be chopped up into patches. The third aim was that the Republika Srpska be contiguous with Serbia so that in the fourth aim it could either join or associate or have some special relationship with Serbia. And the fifth aim was to divide Sarajevo between the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Muslims. And the sixth and last aim was to hold a veto power over any serious actions that would be taken or contemplated by the central government in Bosnia, because they knew there would be a Central Bosnian government since the state had existed. It was already a member of the UN and was recognised internationally. So those were the six war aims of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you talk about the territory and the recognised entity, what became known either then or later as the Republika Srpska, was there any aspect or dimension of the Bosnian Serb objectives or aims having to deal with ethnicity or the demographic make-up of the citizenship, if you will, or the members, the persons who would live in this territory?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. They made it clear, abundantly clear, that their goal was a homogeneous state, a state of Serbs and for Serbs. And one also observed that because we were aware of the ethnic cleansing that was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you're saying now that not only did you come to know that as an objective, but you actually saw conduct -- are you telling us you saw conduct consistent with or evidencing that objective?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Oh, yes. It was probably the most attention-getting activity of the Bosnian Serbs was their ethnic cleansing activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me turn then next to the objectives or aims that you came to know held by the Bosnian Croat party to these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The Bosnian Croats made clear to us that they also wished to have their own entity in -- in and on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was what they called Herceg-Bosna. They had created a -- a unit. It can be called a community, later a republic. They said, "We speak on behalf of Herceg-Bosna." They were quite clear about that, and they also wanted a special relationship with Croatia or the possibility to join Croatia formally at some later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you learn anything about their aims or objectives in terms of geography or territory?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. The principal areas of interest to Mate Boban and the Bosnian Croats were, as you might expect, the areas where Bosnian Croats live, and this was primarily the -- in Herzegovina along the Dinaric mountains, the border between the Dalmatian coast and Bosnia. And the other major region was the Posavina, the area south of the Sava River in Bosnia but directly adjacent to Croatia. And then they had very strong interests in Central Bosnia, areas like Travnik, Jajce, Vares. President Tudjman was particularly interested in Vares. He would raise that subject with me frequently. And so Central Bosnia was also an area of interest. The three areas were Herzegovina, Central Bosnia, and the Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in connection with the territory, did you and Secretary Vance and Lord Owen come to recognise or identify that territory, the desired territory, with any concepts or maps that you had been familiar with before?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, we knew of this Macek-Cvetkovic Agreement, and that was one aspect. And we also learned directly from the parties. We were, after all, negotiating with them about the future of this area, and they made clear what they wanted. Indeed they gave us their own maps. Each of the three parties would periodically bring us map about where they thought the boundaries, if there were to be boundaries - I repeat, if there were to be boundaries - where they were to be set. So we had a direct knowledge from Karadzic, Boban, Izetbegovic, you know, of the areas that were of particular interest to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I should -- may I add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Just to give an example for Your Honours, it was known, and this was a problem between the Muslims, that the Cazinska Krajina, what came to be called during the war the Bihac pocket, but Cazinska Krajina was an area of deep concern to the government because in the Cazinska Krajina was an alternate Bosnian Muslim leader who was no friend of the administration in Sarajevo, and they were no friend of his, a gentleman named Fikret Abdic. And President Tudjman was also keep concerned about the fate of the Cazinska Krajina, the so-called Bihac pocket, not because there were Croats living there, there were very few, but it's the point of Bosnia that juts into Croatia. So it's of direct interest to the Croatian government. And then we must bear in mind that President Tudjman was, after all, a military man and very aware of transport. And as he would say to me more than once, the transportation from -- the roads, the railroads, roads from Zagreb, from Karlovac down to the Dalmatian coast went through the Cazinska Krajina. That is to say, went through Western Bosnia. So these were the constant concerns, and one did not need to infer the importance of areas to the warring parties because they made clear to us what their concerns were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we -- we will look at, in fact, one of the maps at the moment, but can we -- before we go on to the map, in describing the aims or objectives of the Bosnian Serb party, which you did a few minutes ago, and the Bosnian Croat party, which you've just done, can you tell us whether to your knowledge and in your experience were the objectives of those two parties more similar or different?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Excuse me, the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, in terms of their objectives as they became known to you.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. There were similarities. There were congruities with respect to the creation of their own separate state; and second, the possibility of joining the mother state, for the Bosnian Serbs Serbia, for the Bosnian Croats, Croatia, and then for the desire that their states be as ethnically homogeneous as possible. So there were overlaps as between the Bosnian Serb and Bosnian Croat war aims in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask that the witness be provided the Exhibit P 09276, which is the book of maps, and if it's more simple, I can -- the Prosecution can provide that, and specifically map -- I'll ask you to look at map 4, which is page 5 of the actual -- in e-court, I think it's page 5 because of the cover page. Perhaps we could centre the one -- one of the maps more clearly on the page and as much as possible in e-court. Maybe zoom out a bit, just a little bit, if we can. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, several times already this afternoon you have made reference to the Cvetkovic-Macek Agreement or the Hrvatska Banovina. Can you tell the Judges whether the territory you associate with those -- with that agreement and that area, is that shown on the map that is currently displayed, you have in front of you as map 4 to Prosecution Exhibit P 09276?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, that is the map of the Banovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us, when you referred to earlier -- you said there were several territorial aims. There were the area of Herzegovina, Central Bosnia, and an area called the Posavina. Let's start with the last area. If you have a pointer there, if you could point somewhere to the area when you call -- when you say the Posavina, what area are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The Posavina is -- constitutes the border, the extreme eastern, northern border between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it's this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.
