utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just noticed myself I was in e-court, but in order to see what the witness is doing I'm looking at the ELMO, now, view.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness. I think most of us in the court were looking at a different video image than the one you were pointing at. Could you point again at the area called the Posavina.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: May I add --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: -- that it was an area of vital concern also to the Bosnian Serbs because it was the centre of the so-called corridor connecting Belgrade and Banja Luka, that is to say connecting the capital of Serbia with the putative capital of the Republika Srpska. There was much suggestion, heavy, heavy discussion about this area during the entire period of the negotiations. Indeed, it is not resolved to this day the status of parts of the Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can just have a moment. I've given you my book of maps, sir, and I'm looking in e-court for another page of that same booklet. If you'll give me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If -- perhaps if I could have the booklet for a moment it might be quicker. Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to what's been admitted as map 6 of that Exhibit P 09276. Now, on this particular map do you see that the Banovina map, has been overlaid on the territories claimed by the Croatian community of Posavina, and the Croatian community of and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Is there a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you come to know -- did you and Secretary Vance and Lord Owen come to know of this relationship between the territories, the territorial aims of the Bosnian Croat party during the period of your negotiations with them?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. As I previously mentioned, Vares, which is over here north of Sarajevo, was a constant subject raised with me by President Tudjman. Jajce, which I already mentioned, is and was very important. There's a waterfall and a lot of waterpower around Jajce. And from the economic point of view, it's very important both for Bosnia and for Croatia, because much of the electric power in Croatia comes from power plants around the area of Jajce. It also has, of course, for all Yugoslavs of a certain age an importance because it was in Jajce in November 1943, during World War II, that Tito declared the existence of the AVNOJ republic, that is to say the Partisan republic. And that day became the national day of Yugoslavia and was the national day from 1945 till 1991. For all I know, it may still be the national day in Belgrade. But these are very sensitive areas, and so this was well-known. And looking up north, Orasje and Odzak and Bosanski Samac, this area was also very sensitive to Mate Boban and to President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in reference to President Tudjman, can you tell us, and think we're done with the maps unless the Judges have questions about the maps before I have the usher return to her seat. Thank you, Your Honours. Sir, you just mentioned that these -- some of these areas, Vares, the Posavina, were of particular concern to President Tudjman. Did you have various conversations and meetings directly with President Tudjman on these topics, these and other parts of the work you were trying to carry out at the time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did he make known to you his views and the relationship between his views and those of the Bosnian Croat party?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: They were identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how did that manifest itself, or how did you know that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your travels -- well, during the time you were carrying out this mission, the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia or ICFY, did you have occasion to travel about the various parts of the former Yugoslavia at that time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. We visited all the capitals, of course. I would say we travelled more, certainly I did, more in Croatia than in any other area, and that's because the fighting in Croatia was very severe. It preceded Bosnia, so we were there earlier, and then we had created the four UN-protected areas in Croatia which I visited regularly. And that was not hard to do. They were all adjacent to Bosnia. And in Bosnia we were -- largely visited Sarajevo and other areas as well, "Jablanica, Vares, Kresevo, Visoko." Jablanica, Vares, Kresevo, Visoko, several areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you this before moving on to another topic. In your travels in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you see anything, did you observe yourself during your travels anything that manifested itself as showing an orientation or an allegiance to Croatia at any part of Bosnia-Herzegovina where you travelled?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. That was self-evident. On one occasion we travelled by road from Split to Sarajevo because the airport was closed due to heavy Serb shelling, and there were never many flights into Sarajevo, which of course was being besieged by the Serbs. We flew in on UN flights, but in this case we couldn't do even that. So we flew from, I believe, Zagreb. But in any case, we drove from Split to Sarajevo and on the main roads, and we were greeted at the border between Bosnia and Croatia by Mate Boban. And there was a lovely table spread with very good Croatian wine, and we all had a drink and then continued on. And we observed the Croatian flag was flying, the red checker flag, which we were quite used to seeing. And anyway, we proceeded north. We saw some Mujahedin at one point, Muslims from the Arab world with their green headbands and yellow printing in the Arabic alphabet, firing guns into the area, driving by on trucks. One always had the impression that they fired more into the air than against the enemy, but that's a separate subject. And we were able to observe -- in fact, we commented to each other, Secretary Vance and I, at the time that the one felt as though one was in Croatia. It wasn't until we were physically on the outskirts of Sarajevo that you didn't know you were in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how so? I mean, what --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, the attitude. All the people who were with us, the people on the side of the road, the flags that were flying were Croatian. If you stopped to buy a Coke Cola you paid in, kuna, the Croatian currency, not the Bosnian dinar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you about -- let me now ask you if you could go to the first instance to one of your are diaries, Exhibit P 00534. Let me ask you some questions about some entries in your diary, please. And if I can -- if you go to tab -- your tab P 00534, and in particular I'm going to be making references, Ambassador, to the -- what we call the ERN numbers as page numbers, and you will see on each page - and sometimes they're easier to find than others - there's a stamp. These begin with -- all these series of numbers begin with an R, and if I can please ask you to go, in particular, to -- I'll wait for a moment until you catch up. Also a date. The date may help since, of course, the material is in chronological order. So I'm going to be referring you to the 11th of October, 1992. The entry for that date 11th of October begins on page, and again I'm referring to the R number, R0164042. If you'd find that. And then specifically my question to you is on the following page, R0164043, and on the right side of that page, on the right side of your notebook, essentially, at the top of that page starts with the word "Karadzic." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, before I ask you particular questions about your entries, can you remind or tell the Judges, please, what particular meetings or conversations you were having on the 11th of October, 1992, just to put this in context?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, as you can see, we were in Geneva. It was Sunday, and Secretary Vance and I and the head of our working group met with Karadzic. We did so frequently, and this was one of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The entry that I just particularly directed your attention to on the page that starts under the heading "Karadzic," says "Kara." Is K-a-r-a an abbreviation?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: That's Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it says "Main problem, Tito's borders. But if Serbs and Croats are clever, exchange borders voluntarily, this exchange would help." Can you tell us please what was being discussed in that regard?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, yes. He was -- he was essentially describing the Graz Agreement to us. And being a Bosnian Serb, he had no love for Marsal Tito who was half Slovenian and half Croat. So he says that the main problem is Tito's borders. You see, the Bosnian Serbs felt they had been done dirt to by Tito in 1945. In any case, that's what he means, that if the Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Croats are clever, those -- they can cooperate with each other, they can basically have what -- what they talked about at Graz, namely to partition Bosnia between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Immediately under the entry that I just directed your attention to, it says: "(Draws map by hand)" Is that a reference to something you did?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: No, he did. You can see it's under the entry of Karadzic. Yes, Karadzic drew a map what the -- of Bosnia by hand, what Bosnia would look like when it was partitioned between the Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you have any recollection generally of what that map looked like?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Certainly, it was basically the same one that President Tudjman drew in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. I wonder if we could just be clear where the asterisks come from. We do see asterisks at various points throughout this document and, in particular, on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will be happy to inquire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ambassador, you just heard the comment by counsel. Can you tell -- can you tell the Judges what the various asterisk markings on this and other pages of your diaries indicate?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, it's quite simple. They indicate points of particular interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when did you put thee asterisks on your diary?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: At the time they were said or as I looked at the document right after the meeting. So they were identically -- really contemporaneous. And if you look at the asterisks, you can see the points being made there are important points.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me then go back to -- we'll be looking at other entries in your diaries as we continue through your testimony, but let me go back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I'm -- interrupt -- we were talking about maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And the witness gave a somewhat cryptic answer in that he referred to a comparison map that Tudjman drew in 1995, and which I do not think is presently before the Chamber. So perhaps the witness could - could - show, on one of the maps we have, what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour. Your Honour, I believe the gentleman is trying to bring in the so-called map that was on the napkin when Paddy Ashdown, who was heavily drinking at the time and having a conversation with Tudjman, who doesn't speak English, that's the conversation the gentleman is speaking about. And as I understand it, the -- this gentleman was not present at the time. So you do need some foundation. One, did he actually see the map, did he actually see the map, and where is this map? But I -- as far as I know, there's already a decision by the Trial Chamber that this is speculative in nature. The question was what it would look like ten years from now, and so on and so forth. So based on that, Your Honour, I think this is one way of trying to sneak in the work of the Prosecution. Basically, I would imagine, because he has been proofed heavily by the Prosecution because for the first time we're hearing things --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- that are not in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, my thoughts went in the same direction but with a quite different idea. I think that, Mr. Okun, you were there and you saw that map being drawn by Karadzic, and I would like you to look at one of the maps we have here and draw what you have seen yourself at that moment but not reproduced in your diary without any reference to any possible later map drawn by anyone at any occasion. I am fully -- I was very, very careful exactly to avoid what you warn us against, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, before he does that, and I think that he should -- and I think he should do that and I'm sure that the Ambassador's quite capable of doing that, but I want to make a record; Mr. Karnavas is always talking about making a record. Your Honour, it is inappropriate for counsel -- he wants to exclude the testimony, exclude the evidence of this but yet engages in character assassination against a person who is not in the courtroom about heavily drink, about who was doing what and saying what. And, you know, it's ironic that we have this speculation by counsel when, in fact, we have Mr. Ashdown's testimony available to us, and this whole question, this whole -- excuse me. This whole question about drinking and all that was discussed in open court in the other cases. Judge Jorda had all of that in front him. Judge Jorda accepted all this testimony -- testimony was accepted in the Blaskic case, in the Kordic case, in the Tuta Stela case. It is odd -- I have to observe again, it is odd that it was relevant in all those cases but not relevant in this case. But in any event, my point is, Mr. Karnavas should not get up every time on his feet and then attack the witness -- a person who is not here and at the same time say, "Well, we shouldn't look at the actual evidence itself."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Ashdown by his own admission said that the wine was flowing. That's what -- that's a quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may. Let's not perhaps transfer the -- the theatre of war to a place where my questions definitely did not want to put it. And, Mr. Scott, this reaction of Mr. Karnavas was to a question of mine rather than -- than to you raising a point. So could the witness be shown a map and then tentatively, according to his memory, demonstrate what he remembers Mr. Karadzic at -- on the 11th of -- what was it? On the 11th of October, 1992, a Sunday, drew in his presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but I will have to obtain a clean map to do that. I have nothing available to me at the moment without making a copy first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think the -- this witness has a level of faculty of abstraction that any map you take where you have the area on it he will be able to abstract from what he sees there and -- and just from his memory draw that borderline which he recalls, and I see that he's nodding to this --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you want him to draw just on a blank piece of paper of Bosnia and the lines? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I thought you could show him any of the maps we have here which has not too much -- let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have a clean -- I don't have an extra copy of the map in the courtroom. That's my problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And you have no --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you want me to stop and have a copy made and bring it into the courtroom I'll be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That might be a solution had unless anybody has a map which --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a map in my briefcase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Why don't you use it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a simple -- a simple map of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Ambassador. There are two other individuals who would like to take the floor. Mr. Praljak is on his feet and Ms. Alaburic, too. Mr. Praljak, what is it that you wanted to say? And it should concern you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] What does a conversation in 1995 have to do with anything when all international agreements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Not an issue, Mr. Praljak. This is not a necessary intervention. Please, you are disturbing the course of the trial. We are not talking about 1995. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] But we're talking about a plan that President Tudjman apparently had with Ashdown. That was in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It is entirely wrong. We are talking about a map on which Mr. Karadzic on the 11th of October, 1992, drew a line and that is all, and I have said so quite clearly, I think. If you had been attentive, you would have been aware of this. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] That's correct, Judge Trechsel, but at the same time the question is whether that map corresponds to the map from 1995 when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, Mr. Praljak. That is not the question. You may -- you may have this question, but it's not the one that is on the table before the Chamber at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, to conclude.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Perhaps I could contribute to this discussion. In my opinion, Mr. Karadzic's words transcribed here, and they concern the borders of all the republics of the former Yugoslavia. And if we are discussing Tito's borders, we are discussing the borders of all the republics of the former Yugoslavia. If we have a look at the way the territory has been divided amongst the Croats and the Serbs, and if we are aware of the contexts in which they were discussions about Yugoslavia at the time, we know that we're referring to parts of Croatia and Serbia or Montenegro that were intended to be exchanged. Baranja or Prevlaka and towards the border with Montenegro. If we continue to have a look at what Mr. Karadzic was discussing, we can see that he referred to Kosovo, to Montenegro, et cetera. So I think that it's a matter of redrawing the borders in the territory of Yugoslavia as a whole. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have obtained a -- have here an extra copy of a map that we have prepared, which is numbered for the record 0 -- P 09841, and since I have an extra copy I don't mind if the witness marks on that and then we can have it made an IC number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, Witness, if you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could the map first be put directly in front of the witness so the witness can first orient himself and make any markings, and then we can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I make two remarks very brief. First the Security Council, right when Karadzic talked about Tito's borders, he was talking loosely. That's the way Karadzic always spoke, speaking very broadly, about all of Yugoslavia. The map he drew by hand in front of us was of Bosnia alone. A second point, President Tito [sic], in contradistinction to what the learned counsel says about his English, speaks good English. I had numerous conversations with him, sitting more closely to the president than I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Are you talking about Marsal Tito?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, because there was a mistake in the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: President Tudjman did not speak fluent English but he spoke good English, and I had occasion to discuss many matters with him directly in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, with that in mind --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: And on the map -- yes, on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I just -- no one's going to see it right now, but I first want you to do is take a marker -- first look at the map. Make sure that you've oriented yourself to the map?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I'm very familiar with this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I know you are. But what I would like you to do is make -- what the Judges have asked us to do is make markings, so draw the line -- recreate the map as best you can recall. That's what Judge Trechsel has asked you to do. So you're going to be provided a marker.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. Starting in the south it would go along the border of the Neretva, then east to cover the entire Drina valley through Semberija, up to the Posavina, and then across to something like this, and then down along the Una River, so it would be roughly like that. Think of a horseshoe, the best way to describe it. Indeed, the word that Bosnians and others used it. The Bosnian Serbs talked about their horseshoe. So that was the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the line that you've drawn and we --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Excuse me. I should have gone this way with this. Sorry. It included all -- everything that's blue on this map. It included everything that's blue and quite a lot of green. The green is the -- are the Muslim areas, and you'll notice in particular, if I may just for a moment point out the area around the Drina. This was the area of heaviest ethnic cleansing by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, you've drawn -- what you've drawn on the map just so we can now ask some questions about it, the -- I'll use your terminology and say kind of an upside down horseshoe with the top of the horseshoe as a number 5 in the area and the open end of the horseshoe of what would be considered the border, the south-west border of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if you will; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The area outside the horseshoe -- if we talk about the area inside the horseshoe and outside the horseshoe, who -- according to Karadzic and your understanding of the Serb position at the time, who would have the territory outside the horseshoe?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: You mean the non-Serb occupied territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you've drawn a horseshoe?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The area --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Which they call Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who would have the territory outside the horseshoe.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: That is not inside. Yes. That would be Croatian with a -- with a small Muslim area. As I mentioned earlier, one of their war aims was to divide Sarajevo so there would be a portion of Sarajevo and surrounding areas that would be Muslim, and basically the Muslim area, as the Bosnian Serbs envisaged it, would run from Sarajevo on the south to Tuzla which you see in the north-east right next to 4 and 5 you see a green spot. That's Tuzla. So you would go from Sarajevo to Tuzla across to Zenica and then back to Sarajevo. So there would be a very small Diamond-shaped area that the Bosnian Serbs would have accorded to the Bosnian Muslims and the rest of the area outside the horseshoe would be for the Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I'm not sure that we're -- again that's the problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I see what's happening, actually. I think that Prosecution counsel, when he's talking about the horseshoe, he's talking about the line but the witness is understanding the area outside the line. So they're talking about different horseshoes, which is the reason Mr. Scott is looking a bit exasperated because Mr. Okun's answers are not quite matching his questions. They're all to do with horseshoes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart; I do appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, what -- I think counsel's right and that's the problem of sometimes withdrawing maps in the courtroom like this. If I -- if you look -- when I call the inside of the horseshoe the area number 10, I'm saying the area -- see the number 10?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm calling that area inside the horseshoe.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, so am I.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The area outside the horseshoe is the area that has most of number 2, most of number 4. That's outside the horseshoe?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The area outside the horseshoe, 2, 3, 4, 6 going around the perimeter?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yeah, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would that be -- who would that territory --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: That would be Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the area inside the area -- the horseshoe, 10, 9, 7, 5, who would have that territory?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: That would be the area for the Bosnian Croats except for the small diamond that I just described, the area roughly from Sarajevo to Tuzla to notes back to Sarajevo would be a Muslim reservation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. As long as we've engaged in this exercise to this point, perhaps we might as well have you mark this area that you say would be the Muslim area or enclave. So I'm going to ask you now to take the manager and do that as best you can.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: That triangle, in Dr. Karadzic's mind, would be Muslim. The rest of the country would be divided between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Serbs. That was Dr. Karadzic's point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I'm moving away from the map so we're --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel, do you have any additional questions about the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I hope this wasn't too disruptive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if we can go back to the work of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We need an IC number, Your Honour, before we proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have an IC number, please. Can we have the map signed, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will become Exhibit IC 520.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ambassador, could you please put today's date, 2nd April 2007, and also could you please sign the document for us. 2nd April. Mr. Scott, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, moving back to the process of the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia itself, just to bring us back to where we were, we talked about the formation of the conference, the working groups of the conference, who the principal representatives of the three parties were to the conference, and as the work of the conference continued into the fall of 1992, can you tell the Chamber whether something called constitutional principles or constitutional framework was developed in negotiations or discussions with the parties?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. That was an important milestone when the conference developed and put on the table the constitutional framework or constitutional principles, as we usually referred to them. That occurred on 27 October 1992. And these were, as you can understand, framework principles to be the guiding rules, the overall guide for the future of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us kind of in a shorthand way, and we will look at some of these principles as they later evolved in the course of your testimony later, but what were the types of concepts that were involved in these principles?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, Bosnia was to retain its sovereignty within its internationally recognised borders. The state was to be democratic, highly democratic, decentralised. The ethnic principle de-emphasised, that is to say multi-ethnic state, democratically decentralised, and also progressively demilitarised. And the formation on the ground, so to speak, the structure, had 10 provinces, including one for Sarajevo with a special status, and the provinces had a good deal of responsibility in this plan. They did not, however, have the right -- according to the constitutional framework, they did not have the right to establish relations, form relations with any foreign country, nor did they have the right to form relations with any international organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the constitutional principals, just to put the various components of the negotiations, the principal parts, if you will, of the negotiations on the table, so to speak, was the -- we've just spent a few -- some minutes talking about a map. Was the "map" part of the ongoing negotiations, the map of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Oh, yes, indeed. The discussions of the map were continuous and contentious.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was a third significant component of these ongoing negotiations something called the military arrangements?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did that involve?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, that involved the -- as I said, the progressive demilitarisation of the country, complete cease-fire, of course, to start with, the removal and secure cantonment of heavy weapons, military roads, civilian roads. It was a lengthy exercise the development of the military arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, sir, just then as -- again as a matter of the process, can you look at Exhibit P 00752. And I believe I can see from where I am that you have that document. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, it's a Resolution of the United Nations Security Council, number 787, adopted on the 16th of November, 1992, and deals with the -- the situation in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at page 5, paragraph 20 of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were the co-chairmen Secretary Vance and Lord Owen making reports to the Security Council throughout this period?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. You'll notice that paragraph 20 says, and I quote, the Security Council: "Expresses its appreciation for the report presented to the council by the co-chairmen of the steering committee of the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia -" that's Owen and Vance "- and requests the Secretary-General to keep the council regularly informed of developments and of the work of the conference," and of course we did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I now ask you to go back to -- or go to Exhibit P 00829, again one of your diaries. And in particular, in referring to the numbers that have been stamped on the various pages, if you could please find -- and I'll refer to the last four numbers just for simplicity's section. 4173, which appears to be a discussion or a meeting on the 28th of November, 1992. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you first of all set the scene for us as to where and what was this meeting about? Who was the meeting with?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. President Tudjman Secretary Vance and his wife, Lord Owen and his wife, me and my wife, and some -- a few senior members of the Croatian government, Gojko Susak, for example, to enjoy ourselves on Brioni and have -- in a nice beautiful Mediterranean setting to discuss the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, throughout -- perhaps throughout your diaries generally to assist the Judges in reading these documents, and in this entry in particular, there are various entries on the page where you have used the initial -- the capital letters or initials FT. Who is FT?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: FT is the president of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You've also used the capital letters GS. Who was GS?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He's Gojko Susak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who was Mr. Susak?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Susak was President Tudjman's closest advisor and the defence minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Of the Republic of Croatia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, on the -- looking at the document, and again we've got essentially on all these items we've got essentially two pages of your diary side by side copied on one A4 sheet. Looking at the right -- the -- excuse me. Looking at the page on the left, at the bottom of that page, do you see: "FT- Muslims want jihad. "GS- must go getting billions from Arabs." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. On page 4173, on the left -- bottom left side of the page.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Ah, the bottom left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies if I misdirected you.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going to the top of the -- right side of the page, "Croats/Serb relations."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct it says: "All agree they are key to solving ex-Yugo problem"?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "FT says he supports this idea - for more than a decade; even wrote about it." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what was being discussed in this context and what was the subject of Croat/Serb relations?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Two aspects here were being discussed. First of all, the situation in Bosnia. Since that's where the war was, that was the main object of this part of this discussion. And then Tudjman who spoke in broad historical terms made allusion to the history of the former Yugoslavia with respect, of course, to the situation as between the Croat people and the Serb people, because they are two -- overwhelmingly the two majority peoples in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When it's attributed to President Tudjman, you said, "for more than a decade, even wrote about it," what he's talking about?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: He's talking about Bosnia, because he had written about partitioning Bosnia as between the Croats and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then below that entry you have the initials again GS, and that's again Mr. Susak, the defence minister?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "Problem is we can't do it. Looks like collusion and future partition of BiH."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, one sees how frank everybody was in discussion because Gojko Susak says the problem is, you know, it won't look good to do it too openly or even too soon. Saying that's what he means. He says it directly. It would look like collusion --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Collusion between --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Of course, it wouldn't just look like collusion, it would be collusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Collusion between who?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The Croats and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Further down the page GS talks again. It says, "GS stresses need for quiet, serious, contacts with Serbs." What was that about?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, Gojko Susak was a very sophisticated man. He's dead now. He was born in Grude in Herzegovina, so he took a direct strong interest, to put it mildly, a strong interest in the Bosnian Croat cause. He was a Bosnian Croat. He later emigrated to Canada and became a Canadian citizen. He was a very sophisticated man. And so he says here that the way to go about the business of partitioning Bosnia with the Serbs is to do it in a quiet fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you please to then go on to the next page --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, where does it say that? That they're going to partition -- I fail to see that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I answer that directly in order to save time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I want to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to President Tudjman saying he supports the idea. Everybody understood he was talking about partition because the very next person to speak, Gojko Susak, says, "The problem is we can't do it," and that's very clear. He's not talking about NASA and a trip to the moon --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I remind the gentleman that it begins with the lifting of the embargo of arms. You know, that's -- if you look at the continuity of the discussion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I beg your pardon, too, sir Could I ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, perhaps this is better for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wrote it as it happened. I put triple asterisks, for Mr. Stewart's benefit. You notice triple asterisks and underlining this phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ambassador, let me ask the obvious question: Why did you put three or four asterisks on both sides of the page on this part of your note?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Because the Bosnian Croat, or I should say Croat Serbian including Bosnian Croat, Bosnian Serbian desire to partition Bosnia-Herzegovina was well-known and very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to the next page of the document, the -- when I say the next page, it's 4174. The next -- essentially the next two pages of your diary, still dated the 28th of November, 1992. On the left side of the page, please, can I direct your attention to this part, in the section that begins headed on the left side of the page FT. Do you see the part it says, "I discussed BiH with Milo and Izzie."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: That's Milosevic and Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "Before the current war and said there are two possibilities." Why don't you just tell us instead of me reading it. They're your words. It's your writing. What were the two possibilities?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The two possibilities were what President Tudjman called a confederal Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina would exist but there would be -- it would be a deeply divided state with three regions, so to speak. The other one would be more formal where you would divide Bosnia-Herzegovina into three parts. Basically the Serb part -- the Bosnian Serb part joining Serbia and the Croatian -- Croat -- Bosnian Croat side joining Croatia, and then as he says, this would leave a Muslim patch - his word, patch - in the middle. And if Your Honours will recall the map I drew a few moments ago, I sketched out for you the line Sarajevo-Tuzla-Zenica-Sarajevo, that triangle in the middle that's what President Tudjman meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: And if I may say, you notice a few sentences earlier right in the middle, the first thing he talked about, President Tudjman, the first thing that he mentioned was the Cvetkovic-Macek Agreement. You see the sentence, if I may quote: "Croatia is smaller today than when it entered Yugoslavia in 1919 and smaller than in 1939, the Macek agreement." That's the Cvetkovic-Macek Agreement. Macek was the Croat so it's understandable that Tudjman would quote his name and not the Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When going down below that it says, then, after the patch, the Muslim patch it says, "but now after war that's academic." So what was being said in that aspect, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, what he meant there was that there was going to be difficult to achieve because of the -- of the conflict and because of all the assistance the Bosnian Muslims were getting in order to maintain themselves. But it remained a goal. And he goes right on to say -- the very next line says: "The only good solution," this is President Tudjman talking. "The only good solution for Bosnia-Herzegovina was the 1939 agreement. It came after 20 years of failure to deal with Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then Tito disastrously made ABiH and made the Muslims a nation." By that President Tudjman means and of course everybody at the table knew exactly what he meant, that the Muslims in the 1970s were declared to be a constituent people of Yugoslavia because the constituent peoples had specific rights in Yugoslavia. They had group rights, for example. They did not need or ever claim minority rights, that certain rights inhered to the "sastavni ne lod [phoen]," their word for "constituent people." And so elevating the Muslims to the status of a constituent people which Tito's government did in, I believe, 1974 was a serious step, and it empowered the Muslims to a certain point, which President Tudjman objected to, as you see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you then going to -- in -- again using the same numbers, 4176, which appears to be -- you can confirm, please, if it's correct. This is still -- we're still continuing on the 28th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: On the left-hand side, the 28th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes, on the left-hand side. And again we have FT: "Until two months ago Izzie and Muslims, plus Muslims wanted unitary Muslim state (GS: Still do secretly)." Is that Franjo Tudjman and Susak speaking?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was being -- what -- what furthermore -- what further can you tell us the page and tell us as much as -- I don't need to ask you the questions about what's being said here.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, as I mentioned earlier in answer to one of your questions, the goal of the Bosnian Muslim government was indeed a unitary state, sort of one person, one vote. And the reason for that was that by 1991, 1992, the Muslim population already in Bosnia was a plurality of 44 per cent of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina, according to the '81 census, '91 was almost identical, was Muslim, was roughly 31 per cent Bosnian Serbs, and about 18 per cent are Bosnian Croats. So the Muslims had the expectation that they would become a majority and President Tudjman and Susak feared very deeply what would happen if and when the Bosnian Muslims ever achieved a majority in a unitary state. That is, as I said, a highly centralised state. And Susak says they still want this. And then President Tudjman goes on to say the Muslims are saying, and I quote him here, "We weren't ready for the Serbs, but we will be for the Croats." And he then went on to say that Tudjman, who was the -- excuse me. Sorry. That Izetbegovic, who was the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but his formal title was president of the Presidency, because they had a rotating Presidency, and since it rotated it was due to rotate actually in January to the Bosnian Croat on the Presidency, and Izetbegovic and Silajdzic and Ganic said that we're at war now. It's a very serious situation. Because of wartime, you know, I should -- I will retain the Presidency. And this displeased President Tudjman, but he goes on to say, "The Muslims decided that Izetbegovic should continue. We don't care. I recommended," quote unquote, "to Boban that he agree and he did. And the reason I put recommended in quotes, because the president smiled at that point, and when he used the word "recommended," of course he knew that he was saying I told Boban or I ordered Boban. So recommended was a politesse, and -- and that indeed continued. Izetbegovic remained the titular president of Bosnia for years thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just so it's clear, Ambassador, if you can, when you say "recommended," and again in quotes, quote, "recommended to Boban that he agree and he did," that Boban agree to what?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Agree to allowing Izetbegovic to continue in the titular Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As the -- as the president of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I look at the time, and that may be the time to take the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, before we -- I'm going to go way back, I'm sorry, to the beginning very, very briefly just to deal with something. Before I forget, we might as well do it now. In your bundle, if you go back to the very first exhibit, we were talking about the Graz agreement. Exhibit P 00187, because I'm not sure we'll have anyone else here who can identify a couple of items on the document. So I forgot to ask you before. I apologise. On the very -- if you look at the second page of that document, it's in the -- I need the assistance of the usher, please. It's in the other binder.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The second page of the document there is -- it's handwritten. It says, "Dear Colm," C-o-l-m. Do you see that? Sir, if you look at the second page.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, sorry. Apparently the wrong -- my apologies, Your Honour. I'll try to come back to it tomorrow. Some pages are missing. I apologise for that. My apologies to the usher for the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, then going to the P 00829. We're still on the same diary we were looking at before the break, I believe, and if we go to the entry for the 17th of December, 1992, page 4240.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: 4240 did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir. All right. On the top of the right side of the page you have -- it looks like Tudjman/Izzie/something us. I guess us. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And let me just make sure -- because I have -- I think I may have misspoken when I said the 17th. Is this -- is the date in your handwriting is that the 17th or the 27th of --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It's 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. All right. Continuing down and going back to the left side of the page then. It says CRV. Who is CRV?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Vance. If I might go through all of the names. I can do it very quickly for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: CRV is Vance. DLO is Lord Owen. HSO is me. PH is Ambassador Hall. Martti is the head of our working group. Martti Ahtisaari. PGR is Perti Ramturan [phoen] from the United Nations Secretariat. Then we have President Tudjman, Vudi Radic [phoen]. Mate Boban, Gojko Susak, Neven Madry, and Professor Janko was interpreting. That was the Croatian delegation, and the Bosnian was Izetbegovic, Silajdzic, Trnka, their lawyer, Somun --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Slow, slow, slow down a little bit, please, for the purposes of the translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Yes. Ambassador, could you slow down and Mr. Scott could you slow down too since the interpreters are having a little difficult following.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I apologise to the Court. Starting with Tudjman President Tudjman; his Chef de Cabinet, Jure Radic; Mate Boban, Herceg-Bosna. You'll notice I do not say BiH next to Mate Boban because he described himself as from Herceg-Bosna. So that's what I wrote. Defence Minister Gojko Susak. Charge Neven Madry. That is to say the Croatian charge d'affair in Geneva; and the interpreter Professor Janko. From the Bosnian delegation was President Izetbegovic; Haris Silajdzic, his foreign minister; Mr. Trnka, their legal advisor; Mr. Somun, another advisor, and Sabrina who interpreted for the delegation when interpretation was necessary, and she is also President Izetbegovic's daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And underneath that there is then the entry marked CRV, Secretary Vance. "Welcome, where do we stand after December 17th." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just looking at this document, sir, can you just look at your notes and tell us then what was discussed at this meeting as -- looking at the notes and whatever additional recollection that you have that you can share with us.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we had brought the two parties together, that is to say the Croatian side and the Bosnian side in order to work with them and see the way forward and find out what was going on and what was on their minds. This is normal practice in a negotiation, particularly at the highest level. And Secretary Vance welcomed them and the first response was Izetbegovic who said, "there is no complete agreement on the map but we're making progress," getting there means making progress. We have problems with Travnik and Mostar, which meant that there was a direct problem between the Croats and the Muslims, and he gave us a new map. He goes on to say that his new map retains the old opstina boundaries, but he says, "we are willing to change them." Owen says, "That's a good thing; they're not sacrosanct." And Boban comes in and says, our commission, that is the Bosnian Croat side met for days but I quoted him here and underlined it, "We could not agree on basic principles." And he went on to make the case for Herceg-Bosna, as you see he said for example you cannot cut off Herceg-Bosna. It is the heartland of the church and of our people. That was Mate Boban. And he goes on to say, "If we are honest, we will recognise this." And he gives the percentages of Bosnian Croats and Muslims living in Herceg Nova, for example. So this was a profound discussion, an open discussion, and it was no secret for us negotiators to hear this from Mate Boban in Geneva because we heard it from him regularly, and Ahtisaari then asks --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who is Ahtisaari for the record?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: That is Martti Ahtisaari. He worked for us. He was the chair of the working group of the international conference on Bosnia-Herzegovina so he had an important job.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you perhaps remind the Chamber of anything Mr. Ahtisaari is involved in at the current time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, after the conference he went back as an official of the United Nations and then returned to Finland, his native country, where some years ago not too long ago he ran for president and was elected president of Finland. And after he retired from the Presidency of Finland he's involved himself actively in good works in international negotiations. Most recently and currently he is the Secretary-General's lead negotiator on the status of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But in December of 1993 he was part of your team?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. He was -- as I mentioned to you, he was chairman of our working group on Bosnia-Herzegovina. And a very good chairman he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Continuing on -- oh, go ahead --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: So that's Martti Ahtisaari, MA in the middle of the page, asks about the status for the map for Bosnia. Is it and joint map? And Boban responds, no, it has not been agreed upon. And Trnka, the Muslim lawyer -- excuse me -- yes, sorry, yes, President Izetbegovic's lawyer, interjects and says, "It's our compromise proposal." And then I sum up and therefore you'll note parentheses. Mr. Stewart, you will see parentheses down the rest of the page, and that means that I'm not quoting them directly. That is to say I'm not writing as I normally do the direct interchange, but I'm at the table summarising what they're saying as I hear it at the moment, and I write, and this is me writing for myself and Vance: "Inconclusive discussion of Travnik/Kupres area with Martti Ahtisaari pressing and others ducking," that means -- ducking is slang for not responding. And I note this is 11.45 a.m. "Ahtisaari, Martti keeps pressing across the entire of difference. The BiH side appearing quite bored with the proceeding answers every query the same way: It makes economic sense, therefore nearby," et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. They kept talking about the things making economic sense. They -- just to say things that favoured the Bosnian Muslim position. And I note then for myself and I write at the time in capital letters what the BiH map shows is gerrymandering. And if the Court wishes I can explain gerrymandering what it means, otherwise, if it is understood, I will stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, just -- you can explain what gerrymandering-- what you -- when you say gerrymandering write -- excuse me, wrote in your knows gerrymandering, explain that concept or terminology.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I can do it briefly. It's an electoral trick where one side to an election dispute or area moves the area, borders around to favour its own side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you -- sorry go ahead.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: And the origin of the phrase comes from the American revolutionary period in the 18th century when a Massachusetts lawyer named Gerry shifted the borders of Massachusetts so that his party could easily be elected, and it's referred to always as gerrymandering. Again meaning moving the borders to favour your side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And continuing on to the next page in the continuation of this you say Haris?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Haris is Silajdzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Can you just take us through -- down to the end -- if we -- just tell you -- please, if you can just take us down to where you -- then it changes to 1.05 p.m., just to finish up this section?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Okay. Silajdzic entered the conversation. He was the Foreign Minister of Bosnia, spoke perfect English. He had studied in the United States. His English was as good and mine. He spoke often quite passionately. He was deeply concerned, and he was a secularist. He was a very strong secular voice inside the Bosnian Muslim government. Izetbegovic was much more of a religious person. So he comes in aggressive, scornful, scowling. That's the way I described his facial behaviour. And he asks-- well, he queries Ahtisaari, claiming that ethnicity should have no place enjoin of the provincial boundaries. And Tudjman immediately rebutted Silajdzic as regards ethnicity, because President Tudjman did believe that the ethnic factor was important. And then Silajdzic and Susak clash over the facts of history of Bosnia. This goes on for a while. And I note, again parenthetically, a remark of myself to myself and Mr. Vance, "Bad blood here." Boban comes in to say that Mostar and Travnik must be together, that is to say in the same province. Silajdzic, Haris, says everything is wrong -- "Everything is wrong with that." And President Tudjman, laughing, again rebuts Silajdzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you recall anything more particular about what either Boban, Haris, or Tudjman said --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: At that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- at that --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: At that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. What was -- when you say, "Tudjman, laughing," why did you note that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, Boban has just said Mostar and Travnik must be together. Silajdzic is saying ethnicity should play no role in the physical, geographical, administrative subdivisions,. And President Tudjman laughs because he knows that of course it will play a role.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving forward then, this is the 27th of December, 1992. We're leading up to the 2nd of January, 1993, and perhaps you can just introduce that to us in terms of what then happened on the 2nd of January.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: On the 2nd of January the co-chairmen, Secretary Vance and Lord Owen, laid down, tabled for all of the parties, for the three parties, a comprehensive peace plan, a settlement. The plan consisted of the basic framework, the constitutional framework, the map and the third part. The third part of the plan were the military arrangements. That was to January.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In that regard then, please, if I can ask you to find in one of the binders that you have in front of you P 01038, which is the next instalment of your diary. I am told it's in binder 1.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you can find that and particularly the page 4253, which I believe should be the beginning of the entry I hope for --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: 4253 you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, please. It looks like we may have the wrong --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Excuse me, I have a page, but I'm afraid I can't read the number. 429 or is it 5? Can somebody help me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: What date but referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We're trying to find the 2nd of January, but that's not the right page. So give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you could go to -- just give me a moment, please. Sorry. 4253 does seem to work if you can find it. If you can find your entries wherever it begins on January 2nd, 1993. That might be the easiest way to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I -- yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thanks very much. I'm sorry for the confusion. On the right side of that page: "11.10 a.m. to 12.30, pentagonal meeting, BiH meeting of 5 dels," which I assume that's "delegations."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And we won't go through all of them unless the Chamber wants us to, but do you then list again the members of each delegation?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. I listed them and capitalised the chairman of each of the five delegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I'm just going to mention the Bosnian Croat group because earlier this afternoon you did acknowledge that you were having trouble for a moment remembering some of the names. Do you see listed here, under "Boban," Mr. Akmadzic and Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Below the names it says: "CRV," Cyrus Vance, "11.25, reads text of statement." Can you tell us what that was about?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, the text of the statement was the statement that he planned to issue to the press after this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And with that in mind -- hold on one moment, please. Did the meeting start -- by the way looking at the page, perhaps you can just assist, this is anecdotally, did meeting start at 11.10 or at 11.40?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: 11.10, as I noted in my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What happened between 11.10 and 11.40 when Mr. Vance -- or 11.25 when Mr. Vance --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, reading the text of the statement, that he went on to read in its entirety the constitution framework, the nine points, and that took some time. He doesn't speak rapidly. He speaks much more slowly and clearly than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: And then Mate Boban spoke, you know, at some length - I mean not just 30 seconds - about the principles and the map a little bit, but nothing significant because I would have noted it if he said anything significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Can I next ask you to look at P 01047. 1047.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: What date is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 2nd of -- not in your diary, a separate document. Entirely separate . The tab -- if you find the tab for the document.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Sorry. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's all right. It does get confusing at times.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you look at that and then tell us what that document is?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. That is the statement that I refer to of Cyrus Vance at the opening of the pentagonal conference. The only thing it don't include is his reading out of the principles, and that wasn't necessary because everybody had the text of the principles. So as you see, that statement is three and a half pages in length, and they are single spaced. So it took some time to read that out. And if I may, for the benefit of the Court --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: -- and yourselves, point out that -- Mr. Vance's remarks at the opening of the second paragraph. I quote: "The process we are starting today." Now one might ask: The conference has been working since early September. Why is Secretary Vance saying -- talking of "the process we are starting today"? He meant the process that began with the formal presentation of the peace plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Looking down the page, please, after -- in the paragraph that starts, "We expect that the outcome," and then below that you have some bullet items. In the first bullet item, if you will, it says: "You agreed to the principles of the international conference adopted on August 26." Can you briefly comment on that, what those principles were?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, those are the constitutional principles that we've talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Next bullet item: "You agreed in London on a number of things, including full and permanent cessation of hostilities, recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the former Yugoslavia republics, respect for the integrity of present frontiers unless changed by mutual agreement." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And have --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, may I revert to the first point, the principles. You'll note the date August 26. The Court will recall that I said the constitutional framework was introduced on October 27. Both are correct. The rough outline of the principles were agreed upon at the London conference on August 26, 1992. The formalised statement of the principles which were in the plan were the ones of October 27. That explains the discrepancy in dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me before leaving this document if you go to the second page and if we continue on the so-called bullet items, it will be overall the fourth bullet item that the second bullet item on page 2 saying: "The three Bosnia-Herzegovina sides also agreed to the unconditional and unilateral release, under international supervision, of all civilians detained, and the closure of detention camps without delay." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And does that relate back to -- much earlier this afternoon you were talking about -- one of the issues that was known at the time was the detention of civilians?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to turn to the bundle or the -- excuse me, the exhibit which is marked P -- well, it's marked 1116. For the record, Exhibit P --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you look on that page, because this is a UN publication, on that page begins -- on the right side of the page, do you see document S/25100?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it may be helpful to just briefly say what that nomenclature terminology means or what numbering system that is. S/25100?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: S stands for secretariat, and 25100 is their numbering. The UN, not surprisingly, numbers their documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. When you look at that entire report it then starts there and continues over the next several pages including ending with -- on a -- page 40 of the document, numbers of pages on the document itself would be page 40, appendix 3. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is that all a report in connection with the meetings in early January 1993?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. This is in fact the text of what came to be called the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, and you will notice that appendix 1 are the constitutional principles with 10 points and the -- it -- the appendix 3. Well, it continues along the road of outlining -- outlining the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we come back further and talk about the positions of the various parties in response to this plan, if we look at appendix 1, the second principle is: "The provinces shall not have any international legal personality and may not enter into agreements with foreign states or with international organisations." Can you tell us the significance -- why was that considered to be one of the top 10 principles at issue here?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It was a vital issue because both the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Croats had made no secret of their desire to have their own states inside Bosnia-Herzegovina and to unite formally or informally with the mother countries, respectively Serbia and Croatia. And the co-chairmen wanted strongly to assure that this did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In that regard, please, can I ask you and everyone in the courtroom please to go back to page 39, to the text of the report itself. And on page 39 there is a section, Roman numeral -- I believe Roman numeral II, resumption of the peace talks. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I please direct your attention to paragraph 9 in that column at the bottom. I know the print is small, and I apologise for that. Can you read what paragraph 9 says?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. Should I read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: "With regard to principle number 1, the co-chairmen commented that they did not see any real difference between what they had proposed and what Mr. Karadzic had offered. The differences appeared to be mainly semantic. Both co-chairmen and Mr. Ahtisaari made it clear, however, that the concept of a 'state within a state' would not be permit the under principle number 1. In response to a comment by Mr. Silajdzic, the co-chairmen reaffirmed that Bosnia and Herzegovina was to remain an independent sovereign state within its internationally recognised boundaries."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you then go on to paragraph number 10 at the top of the next column.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Paragraph 10 reads: "With regard to principle number 2, which was omitted from Mr. Karadzic's list, Mr. Ahtisaari explained that it was not intended to restrict the role of the provinces on matters within their competence. In this regard, he read the following statement which he stated would form part of the records of the conference explaining principle number 2."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just in the interest of time and everyone has the entire document in front of them, can you just refer to the first two sentences of that next section?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. The first two sentences read as follows: "Only Bosnia and Herzegovina is to have an international legal personality. Provinces cannot conclude formal international treaties."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Directing your attention, please, back to Appendix 1 on page 40. And if I can just ask you briefly to look at principle number 8. Can you just read that and make any additional comment that you can about principle 8?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Principle number 8 reads always follows: "Bosnia and Herzegovina is to be progressively demilitarised under United Nations/European Community supervision." I should say it speaks for itself, but I would add that in January 1993, it's important never to forget that the conflict was still continuing. There was heavy fighting in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: While we have that text in front of us and before going on to something else, can you tell the Judges, looking at that language, and then I'll ask you more generally, was there anything about the Vance-Owen proposals as they existed on the 2nd of January, 1993, which talked about the withdrawal or subordination of any particular military units in any particular territories?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, there was a very large section on military arrangements, and I mentioned withdrawal was discussed, but there is nothing in -- in that document, in the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, that spoke about subordination of units with respect to withdrawal. The most detail in the agreement concerned the removal and cantonment of heavy weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me -- without having looked at the documents, and everyone now has the entire Vance-Owen record -- agreement as it existed as of the 2nd of January in front of them, what was the reaction of the three principal parties, the Bosnian Croats, the Bosnian Muslims, and the Bosnian Serbs, to this proposal?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The Bosnian Croat side accepted the entire proposal. The Bosnian Muslim side accepted the principles, accepted but did not sign the military arrangements. So that was a conditional acceptance. And rejected the map. The Bosnian Serb side rejected the Vance-Owen proposal, all three principle sections. They rejected in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was the -- what happened after, then, this important meeting on the 2nd of January?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, we returned -- we kept negotiating. I mean, the goal was to reach agreement of all three parties, so the conference went back to the negotiating table.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you -- you talked earlier this afternoon about -- that some of the Bosnian Croat and Bosnian Serb interests were similar, or "congruent" I think was the word you used at one point. Was there an interplay here in the positioning of the -- the positioning and posturing of the various parties in relationship to each other and, in particular, between the Croats and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I would say there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, both sides would publicly express deep concern about the conflict, their regret that it occurred, their desire to end the conflicts, their hope to live in peace and eternal harmony forever and ever, and at the same time they were carrying out on the ground a very different policy and that was this two-track policy. There was the difference that -- the attention, I would say, of the broad public was largely focused - and correctly - on the Serb activities inside Bosnia, because it was the Serbs, for example, who had besieged, were besieging Sarajevo and firing many shells into the city on a daily basis. The UN, if I may parenthetically add, kept an accurate account of the number of shells fired by General Mladic and his troops into Sarajevo, and it averaged 5.000 a day. So that was the main attention, and it was widely known there Karadzic who said publicly that they would reject the Vance-Owen Plan. That was -- that was known.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How did the Serb rejection of the Vance-Owen Plan in its entirety impact the negotiating positions of either the --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
