utterances.text: Well, it gave both the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, particularly the Bosnian Croats, a free ride, because they could accept the Vance-Owen Plan in the secure knowledge that it would not go anywhere because of Bosnian Serb rejection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your negotiations and discussions with the three parties, and in this particular instance the Bosnian Croat delegation, did you have any understanding of the reasons or motivations as expressed or as observed by you as to their agreement to the parts of the Vance-Owen Plan in January?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. We knew that they were not just formally happy with the proposed map. In reality, they were quite pleased with the map. Vance-Owen took strong account of the needs of the Bosnian Croat people. So the map was fine with Mate Boban. The military arrangements they didn't talk much about, and we knew that reason. And again, they knew that the focus on the military, as I mentioned earlier, was going to be on the withdrawal of heavy weapons, and that meant Serb gunners bombing, shelling Sarajevo and other cities. So that one was easy for them to accept. And they did not like the principles but went along with them because they knew, again, that there would have to be, or they thought there would have to be, some adjustment in the principles if the co-chairmen were to gain Serb acceptance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, when you say just now they didn't -- they did not like the principles but went along with them, and then, as you further said, in what ways did they not like the principles. How did that show that --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, above all they did not like the point 2 about not having an international personality and not having any -- "may not enter into agreements with foreign states or with international organisations," and that directly had a very harmful impact on their desire, which we've discussed earlier, to either join Croatia at a later date or have a special relationship with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It may be -- excuse me. All right. I asked you earlier, then, did negotiations continue on in light of the various positions that you've just explained? And let me ask you to look in particular, please, at -- again, Exhibit P 01038, which is again part of your -- one of the parts of your diary.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can ask you to please find page 4266.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: What date is that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. The 4th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: January 4th. Yes, I have January 4th. What -- 4266. Yes, I have it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me catch up with you for a moment. You're ahead of me in this instance. Thank you very much. Okay. You have that. This is an additional meeting on the 4th of January, 1993, and you've again listed the various persons who participated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the right -- excuse me. On the left side of the page you have a reference -- an entry for Izzie.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: That's President Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what does he say there, and can you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I quote what I wrote: "President Izetbegovic asks for an additional principle that Bosnia-Herzegovina is a sovereign independent recognised country." It was. Everybody knew it. The -- the chairmen, the co-chairmen, felt it was self-evident that Bosnia was an independent country. It was a member of the UN, that it did not need saying, but Izetbegovic was clearly nervous about that and asked that it be included.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On page 4267, the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There's a reference to something said by Mr. Vance. CRV with two of your asterisks next to it. "Reads prepared texts. Puts two inextricably linked documents on table: A, cessation of hostilities; and B, constitution and map."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, that's very easy to explain. The three parts of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan that we've mentioned, the constitutional principles, the map, the military arrangements, were to be accepted as a package, that is to say all three. So we needed nine signatures. Three parties, three principals, nine signatures. And we had three. The Bosnian Croats had accepted. But -- and then we had this semi-conditional acceptance by Izetbegovic. So Mr. Vance wanted to make clear to all parties, but particularly to the Muslims and Serbs, that they one not be allowed to pick and choose which of the parts of the peace plan they liked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the right side of the page there's a number of entries, and again everyone has the entire page and can read everything. The middle of the page, Boban, basic thing is "justice. We have no right not to create peace," I think it says. All three parties, "We accept this package." And it's attributed to Izetbegovic, "Izzie, we are ready to sign without map." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that even by the 4th of January, 1993, there was still no agreement between the three parties?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, there was no agreement between the two [sic] parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can go -- I believe it's in the same part of your diary, but if you can find page -- I'm going to make sure. 4280.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. Dated January 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. "Meeting of the five parties, second round." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in that set of minutes and notes -- sorry. Forgive me. I'm looking for the entry. Sorry. It's on page 4287. If you can go forward in the same -- again, still on the 10th, but the notes go on for some period of time. I'm sorry. At the end of the 10th of January meeting, the next day goes on to the 11th of January, on page 4287. Is Boban -- is it correct that your notes indicate Boban: "I believe they don't want a map at all. We must insist on constitutional text that Muslims accept map."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise for the confusion but if you find --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: My pages are not numbered, counsel, so I'm having difficulty following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I have 4286.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you go to the next page hopefully --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, it does not say so but I assume it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I apologise if that's not clear. On that next page on the left-hand side, if you go down, do you see an entry next to Boban?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Is that the one that says, I quote, "We had the feeling that Silajdzic wanted to break up the talks"? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Above -- well, I don't know. I'm looking at 4287. Perhaps the usher can assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The witness was looking at the right hand page of the previous page. He's looking at the little right-hand page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Turn the entire A4.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Boban, yes, I see that. I have that page. I apologise to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Since it's been a couple of moments now, can you just read the -- the note that you've attributed to Mr. Boban on that page?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, if we back up a little bit you see that Mate says, "the Muslims want to end the talks. They forget the principles -- they forget that the principles and the map are one unit." And he's quite right. That's what Mr. Vance said when they are inextricably linked. And then Mate continues by saying at the top of the next page: "Even with the war," and I write "et cetera" meaning the war and the fighting and the killing just the usual words, "we must take into account legitimate Serb claims."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: And that again is telling us that some of the Bosnian Serb claims are legitimate, and he means -- and he knows we know that he means the Serb claims to their own state and to their own territory, because they were identical to his aims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, that was my next question to you. Why would Mr. -- why would Mr. Boban be claiming the legitimacy of Serb claims?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I think I've just answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you say it again, please?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: In Mate's mind, Mate Boban, that is, the "legitimate Serb claims" were those that were congruent or identical with the Bosnian Croat claims, specifically the desire to have a separate state within the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then below that the next -- there's -- not the next one but the -- do you see the entry "Boban: I believe."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you read that to us, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, Secretary Vance had said, "What about the Bosnian team and the map?" And Mate Boban responded, and I quote: "I believe they don't want a map at all. We must insist in the constitutional text that the Muslims accept the map. They won't accept Sarajevo province, but will accept a tripartite Sarajevo city." By that he meant that province number 10, it was called number 10 on the Vance-Owen map, was to be the area of Sarajevo and the surrounding provinces, and it was to have a separate status to be under strict tripartite rule, that is to say Bosnian Muslim, Bosnian Croat, Bosnian Serb. And that's what he meant when he said, "they will not accept tripartite."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did the concept -- because this may relate to something that may come up tomorrow, was there always a different concept as to how the area around Sarajevo would be organised or governed under the plan?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: There were differing opinions. You might call them concepts although that's a rather elevated term for the way the parties felt. The Muslims took the strong view that Sarajevo was theirs, it was their capital, and that nobody else should really have a look in on the rule of Sarajevo. This concerned primarily the Bosnian Serbs, because the Bosnian Serbs had a heavy presence, a large population, in Sarajevo. It was of much less concern to the Bosnian Croat side because very few Bosnian Croats lived in Sarajevo compared to the other two nationalities. An additional difficulty was that the mountains around Sarajevo were largely Bosnian Serb populated. Ilidza, for example, and some others. And Pale, for example, which is where the Bosnian Serbs installed their pseudo-government. So they had an interest in both the city of Sarajevo and the bowl, I -- if I may describe it, the rim around the city, which was occupied by Serbs. And then there was the fact on the Bosnian Serb side that their number-two man, Momcilo Krajisnik, was himself from Sarajevo and had a real feeling towards the city. Karadzic, for example, did not. He's a Montenegrin by origin, and to him Sarajevo was just another city. But Krajisnik, who played an important role in the Bosnian Serb affairs was, very strong on Serbs retaining an important role in Sarajevo. You'll recall, Your Honours, that I mentioned as one of the Bosnian Serb war aims the partition, the division of Sarajevo. So it was an important issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you next, please, to go to the next page. It should be the next -- very, very next page in your diary, starting on the 12th of January.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Excuse me, I have January 20th as the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. I don't know why we seem to be having so much difficulty?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Are you talking about 4307?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No I'm talking about 4297.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry, I don't have it in this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It may be in the next binder?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Ne je sais pas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It may be in the next binder, please. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, it's the same here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for the difficulties, and it's five to 7.00. Maybe the best thing to do is to end now and see if we can hopefully make this clear overnight. I apologise for the confusion. Mr. President, that would be my suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ambassador, we are finished for today. As you know, you will be testified over the next four days, until Thursday. Since we will be sitting in the afternoon, tomorrow I kindly ask you to come back at the session starting at 2.15. I am inviting everybody else to come back tomorrow for our afternoon session starting at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 3rd day of April, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
